title: ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute – Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs

paper.title: ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute – Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a
containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or
execution results, and determines its later actions by those
earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead:
their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and
the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain
earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the
repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment’s outputs. We present ANTE
(Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the
policy’s pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into
per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an
internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy
Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step
advantages by anchoring credit on the policy’s own forecasts. To turn
the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby
facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among
candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model’s accuracy climbs from
44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers
across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.15368v1 [cs.LG] 11 Oct 2026 \authoremails yige@umd.edu , kangruir@amazon.com ANTE: Anticipate, Then Execute – Learning Internal World Models for Coding Agents from Verified Beliefs Yi Ge Affiliation: University of Maryland, College Park Work done during an internship at AWS AI Labs Kangrui Ruan Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Corresponding author Jifan Chen Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Manish Prajapat Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Christian Bock Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Xiaoyang Wang Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Rein Houthooft Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Aritra Sengupta Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Varun Kumar Affiliation: AWS AI Labs Abstract Rapid advances in large language models have made software engineering agents capable of tackling complex coding tasks. Within a containerized environment, a coding agent receives tool responses or execution results, and determines its later actions by those earlier results. However, most existing coding agents never look ahead: their policies do not anticipate the consequences of actions, and the terminal reward barely attributes a failure to certain earlier steps, so an ill-judged edit can corrupt the repository state irreversibly before any signal arrives. Recent code world models aim to address these challenges, but they are either trained and then frozen before reinforcement learning (RL), or reduced to an auxiliary next-token loss on the environment’s outputs. We present ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute), an agentic RL framework that verifies the policy’s pre-action predictions by real execution and turns them into per-step credit for its actions and trust-or-abstain decisions. With an internal belief stated before each action, Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO) turns the settled predictions into per-step advantages by anchoring credit on the policy’s own forecasts. To turn the trained forecasts into better actions at inference, thereby facilitating effective test-time scaling, ANTE-TTO (test-time optimization) selects among candidate actions without an external scorer. ANTE raises Qwen3-32B from 25.0% to 57.2% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, 6.2% above a matched GRPO baseline trained without the belief state; its world model’s accuracy climbs from 44% to 69% during RL, and the learned foresight capability transfers across harnesses and out-of-distribution domains. In summary, we aim to build a code world model that knows what has happened, what holds now, and what the next action will achieve. † † Project Page: https://ante-agent.com 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) now act as software engineering agents: given a repository issue or a terminal task, they edit, run, and iterate inside a container until tests validate the result ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Pan et al., 2025 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) . Open agents are trained by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on executed trajectories ( Yang et al., 2025b ) and by reinforcement learning (RL) against that terminal test ( Song et al., 2026 ) , at growing scale. Both SFT and RL are trained on tool-use trajectories, in which the agent observes each tool result and uses it to choose the next action ( Luo et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025c ) . However, outcome-based RL rewards only the final task result ( Shao et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025c ; Ding et al., 2026 ) ; it does not directly train the agent to predict what each action will do. Without anticipating an action’s consequences, an agent may solve the immediate problem while introducing errors elsewhere in the repository. Figure 1 illustrates this limitation: both the reactive agent (thinking-only) and the retrospective agent (thinking with memory) submit an edit that passes the target test but breaks a previously passing test. The memory records what happened, but neither agent anticipates the edit’s side effects before acting. To anticipate such failures, an agent needs to predict an action’s outcome before executing it. A world model provides this prediction, which can then be checked against the execution result, such as whether a test will pass. The observed outcome then serves as a training target, helping the world model make more accurate predictions. Existing approaches learn from execution traces or auxiliary observation losses ( Meta FAIR CodeGen Team, 2025 ; Shrivastava et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) , or refine simulated plans ( Yu et al., 2025b ) , but do not turn verified forecasts into per-step policy credit. Other approaches rely on learned simulators or language-model judges to evaluate predictions ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Execution-verified reasoning has been explored within individual programs ( Ni et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026a ) , rather than repository-level agent trajectories. The remaining gap is to combine explicit forecasts, verification by real execution, and per-step credit within agentic RL. Figure 1: Anticipation, verified by execution. Top: the same task with and without a belief state; only ANTE forecasts the edit’s effect and lets execution settle it before committing. Bottom: under RL, resolve rate and prediction hit rate rise together. We introduce ANTE (Anticipate, Then Execute) , an agentic RL framework that trains coding agents to predict action outcomes and learn from execution feedback. Before each action, the policy writes a belief state containing a brief state summary, an outcome prediction, and a trust or abstain decision. Our code world model maintains an internal belief about what the agent has established, what the code does now, and what the next command will change. During RL, ANTE utilizes Belief-Anchored Policy Optimization (BAPO), which compares steps across rollouts that predict the same outcome and assigns per-step credit based on their verified forecasts and trust decisions. At inference, ANTE-TTO samples alternative actions when the policy abstains or predicts failure, ranks the candidates by their own forecasts, and executes the highest-ranked action without an external scorer. Figure 1 illustrates how this helps: unlike the reactive and retrospective agents, ANTE anticipates that the proposed edit would break other tests, chooses an alternative fix, and confirms that the full test suite passes. This example illustrates the behavior we seek: anticipating an action’s consequences rather than reacting to them afterward. Our main contributions are: ❶ To our knowledge, ANTE is the pioneering agentic RL framework in the code domain that verifies the policy’s explicit forecasts against real execution throughout RL. These verified forecasts provide step-level supervision for learning an internal world model within the policy. ❷ To turn verified predictions into per-step credit, we propose BAPO. It groups steps across rollouts by their predicted outcomes and compares their execution feedback, allowing individual steps to receive credit beyond the final task reward. ❸ We also propose ANTE-TTO, which uses the learned forecasts to choose among candidate actions before execution at inference time. It ranks candidates by their predicted outcomes and executes only the highest-ranked action. At 7B scale, it improves task success rate with approximately 31% additional inference tokens over a single greedy attempt. ❹ Our experiments show that ANTE improves both prediction accuracy and task performance across tasks and harnesses. ANTE-32B reaches 57.2% on SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , outperforming all compared open-weight agents above 30B. ANTE-9B reaches 24.7% on Terminal-Bench 2.0 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) . In addition, across eleven out-of-distribution benchmarks, ANTE-32B improves average performance by 6.2 percentage points over a matched RL baseline trained without the belief state. 2 Related Work World models for coding agents. Code world models could help coding agents anticipate the consequences of their actions. CWM ( Meta FAIR CodeGen Team, 2025 ) learns to predict program execution during mid-training, while its RL stage does not reward or check these predictions. SWE-World and PatchWorld ( Sun et al., 2026 ; Bai et al., 2026 ) instead model the environment outside the policy, as a learned simulator or an executable program. ECHO and PaW ( Shrivastava et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2026 ) add an auxiliary loss on the environment’s outputs during RL, yet the policy still acts without first stating a forecast. In contrast, ANTE has the policy forecast each action’s outcome before acting, verifies the forecast by real execution throughout RL, and uses it for per-step credit and, at test time, for ranking candidate actions. Structured beliefs in agentic RL. Prior work rewards an agent’s beliefs during RL by comparing them with the true state, through a language-model judge ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Singh et al., 2026 ) or embedding similarity ( Yu et al., 2026 ) . However, such comparisons only approximate correctness, and judge-based rewards are prone to reward hacking ( Wang et al., 2025b ; Yu et al., 2026 ) . T3 ( Zou et al., 2026 ) keeps the belief implicit and truncates rollouts once proxy signals show that it has stalled, leaving the belief itself unsupervised. ANTE grounds the belief in verifiable action outcomes, which makes the supervision more robust: real execution checks each forecast and the decision to trust it. Credit assignment and execution-grounded reasoning. Deciding which steps across rollouts are comparable is central to per-step credit assignment. GiGPO ( Feng et al., 2025 ) compares actions taken from the same environment state, which requires identical states to recur across rollouts. ReBel ( Tang et al., 2026b ) groups steps whose beliefs agree on a set of predefined predicates, while PRIME ( Cui et al., 2025 ) instead learns an implicit process reward model that gives dense rewards. Code-reasoning methods use execution traces within individual programs rather than repository-level agent trajectories ( Wang et al., 2026 ; Tang et al., 2026a ; Ni et al., 2024 ) . Our proposed BAPO also compares steps that make the same forecast in different rollouts of the task. 3 ANTE: Learning to Predict Before Acting Figure 2: Overview of ANTE. In Stage I, the model learns the belief state from execution-labeled BeliefTraj; Stage II verifies every forecast against execution and turns it into a prediction loss, a decision reward, and BAPO step credit; ANTE-TTO resamples at an abstention or a predicted fail and executes the best-forecast candidate. 3.1 Problem Formulation We formalize a coding agent working on a task inside its container as a partially-observable Markov decision process (POMDP) ( Åström, 1965 ; Kaelbling et al., 1998 ) whose latent state includes the repository (Appendix A ). We train and evaluate ANTE on two agent harnesses: repository issues under R2E-Gym ( Jain et al., 2025 ) at 7B, 14B, and 32B, and terminal tasks at 9B with the Tmax agent ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) . The 7B and 14B models build on Qwen2.5-Coder-Instruct ( Hui et al., 2024 ) , the 32B model on Qwen3-32B ( Yang et al., 2025a ) , and the 9B model on Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) . The belief schema and the advantage are the same on both harnesses; the outcome space, the anchor key, and the decision reward are set per harness (§ 3.1 , Appendix I ). Data and Comparisons. SFT uses paired corpora containing 12,500 verified successful trajectories over 6,729 repository tasks and 30,161 over 10,823 terminal tasks from the tmax-15k pool ( Ivison et al., 2026 ) . We compare ANTE with two controlled baselines: Reactive , which follows a conventional agent-training paradigm in which the policy interleaves thinking and tool calls; and Retrospective , which augments Reactive with an explicit memory state summarizing the trajectory so far. Neither includes ANTE’s outcome forecasts or trust/abstain decisions. Their paired SFT corpora share source trajectories and tool calls. Each variant then generates fresh on-policy rollouts from its own SFT checkpoint using matched RL pools of 6,566 repository tasks and 3,558 terminal tasks. To ablate BAPO, we additionally evaluate ANTE (w/o BAPO), which retains the belief state and prediction loss but uses episode-level policy advantages without decision rewards or belief-anchored step adjustments. Evaluation. We evaluate on SWE-bench Verified ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ) , on three terminal benchmarks (TB-Dev, TB-Lite ( OpenThoughts-Agent team et al., 2026 ) , and Terminal-Bench 2.0 ( Merrill et al., 2026 ) ), and on eleven out-of-distribution reasoning benchmarks. The RL baselines train the same corrected group-relative objective in the same setting, with the belief components removed. Each starts from the SFT checkpoint of its own corpus variant, so every matched pair isolates the belief. ANTE-TTO also runs one trajectory per task: at each trigger step it samples K = 3 K=3 alternatives at temperature 1.0, scores them by their beliefs, and executes only the winner (§ 3.4 , Appendix G ). All other entries are single greedy attempts (temperature 0). The world model sharpens and the trust decision is learned. To understand the behavior that yields these results, we analyze ANTE’s trust decisions, the relationship between its beliefs and task outcomes, and representative trajectories. Figure 5 traces the belief through RL. The hit rate of conclusive predictions rises at every scale (a), from 44% to 69% at 32B, so the forecasts the policy acts on become more accurate as training proceeds. The trust rate doubles (b), the accuracy of trusted predictions rises past q ∗ q^{\ast} , the level above which trusting is rewarded (c), and abstention concentrates on the steps that remain uncertain (d). The belief also outperforms SWE-World’s dedicated 32B reward model ( Sun et al., 2026 ) as a judge of its trajectories (Table 11 ). Together with the ANTE-TTO gains of Table 2 , this is the empirical side of Proposition 2 . RL lowers the forecast error that bounds the selection regret, the forecasts carry outcome signal, and selecting by them raises success. The foresight is therefore not only predictive but also actionable. Case study. Figure 6 shows how the three models handle a repository issue. In this case, uploading a file with the method u’POST’ , a Unicode string, raises a UnicodeDecodeError . The fix is to convert the method to the native string type, which is bytes on Python 2 and str on Python 3. Reactive reasons only about the immediate error and encodes the method to bytes. It is not aware of the environment the fix must run in, so when Python 3 rejects the bytes method, it dismisses this as outside the issue and submits the fix. For Retrospective, the memory records only past steps and indicates nothing about what its bytes edit will do. ANTE’s belief predicts what the next edit will change. It scopes the bug to Python 2 (“force bytes in py2”), so it uses the existing native-string helper instead of forcing bytes everywhere. This foresight ability makes ANTE resolve tasks more robustly (full trace in Appendix N ). 5 Conclusion With ANTE, we want coding agents to foresee the consequences of their actions and to let real execution correct their beliefs. During training, ANTE’s world model forms an internal belief within the policy: what the agent has established, what the code does now, and what the next command will change. The foresight ability lets ANTE improve across harnesses and model scales, and generalize to tasks in other domains. In summary, we envision agents whose beliefs span their environment’s past, present, and future, acting on what they anticipate and learning from what execution reveals. Coding tasks and execution-based verification. A repository issue ( Jimenez et al., 2024 ; Jain et al., 2025 ) consists of a containerized repository at a fixed commit, an issue description, and a hidden test suite 𝒰 \mathcal{U} . It is resolved when the submitted patch passes every fail-to-pass and pass-to-pass test in 𝒰 \mathcal{U} . A terminal task states a goal in natural language inside an isolated container, and a hidden checker grades the final state. In both harnesses, each step is one assistant message that reasons and then makes exactly one tool call, and the environment replies only in text. Execution can check one part of the belief exactly: the deterministic verifier ψ \psi of § 3.1 ( Jain et al., 2025 ) maps each response to an outcome in 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} , or to ⊥ \bot when it determines none.
